newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine, IMF agree deficit increase in 1997-dep PM.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine, IMF agree deficit increase in 1997-dep PM.

text.p: Ukraine and the International Monetary Fund have reached an agreement under which the country could raise its budget deficit to four percent of GDP from three in 1997, the deputy prime minister announced late on Tuesday.

The agreement, linked to a promise by Ukraine to implement tax reform next year, paves the way for the former Soviet republic to receive a three-year, $2.5-3.0 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) loan in 1997.
"We had big problems trying to raise the deficit in talks with the IMF," said Viktor Pynzenyk during a late-night television announcement.
"But after complex discussions we were able to persuade IMF representatives, and to reach an agreement allowing us to raise the deficit to four percent by Western calculations," he said.
The EFF would succeed an $867 million stand-by programme when it runs out early next year, but the IMF board would not grant final approval until next month or even early next year.
President Leonid Kuchma has repeatedly promised to begin long-awaited tax reform next year.
Ukraine's original draft budget for 1997 had proposed a deficit of 3.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), or three percent by Western calculations.
The new agreement, reached after an IMF mission completed a three-week visit to Kiev, allows Ukraine's deficit to grow to 5.8 percent of GDP, or four percent by Western calculations.
"The increase will not be covered by the printing of money but through foreign credits," Pynzenyk said.
Ukraine's three-year government plan, announced in September, envisaged $2.5 billion in foreign credits in 1997.

The draft budget, to be reviewed by the government this week and then by parliament, had not specified precisely how Ukraine would cover the deficit. The original draft envisaged a split almost evenly between foreign credits and sales of Treasury bills.
Ukraine's new constitution states that the budget must be passed by parliament by January 1.
Deputies in parliament, many of them left-leaning, have indicated they would not support the new budget if it continues to follow the tight fiscal policy of this year and last.
Ukraine has succeeded in reining in inflation to a forecast 40 percent this year from 182 percent in 1995.
The draft budget sees 25 percent annual inflation in 1997 and modest growth -- the first since Ukraine became independent in 1991.
